content: The recommendations were reviewed and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) before publication. The development of these recommendations involved assessing the certainty of evidence for each question using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The GRADE approach evaluates factors such as risk of bias, study limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication/reporting biases. The GRADE system categorizes the certainty of evidence into four levels: 1. High certainty: The group is very confident in the estimated effect, and further research is unlikely to change this confidence. 2. Moderate certainty: The group has moderate confidence in the estimated effect, but further research is likely to have a significant impact on this confidence and may change the estimate. 3. Low certainty: The group has low confidence in the estimated effect, and further research is very likely to have a significant impact on this confidence and is likely to change the estimate. 4. Very low certainty: The group is very uncertain about the estimated effect. When selecting topics for inclusion in the guideline, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) Secretariat and Steering Committee consulted several existing guidance documents. Members of the Steering Committee and GDG agreed to incorporate recommendations from two existing guidelines. The first set of recommendations was derived from the Guideline on Hand Hygiene in Health Care in the Context of Filovirus Disease Outbreak Response: Rapid Advice Guideline (November 2014). These recommendations were based on the 2009 WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care and a systematic review of three key research questions, followed by a GDG meeting in November 2014. However, the systematic reviews conducted for the 2014 guideline did not identify comparative studies on the use of bleach/chlorine solutions versus alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water for hand hygiene or glove disinfection. Limited evidence was available on adverse reactions to bleach/chlorine solutions for hand hygiene, but additional information was inferred from reports on their use for other purposes. Only one study examined the effect of chlorine solutions on glove permeability, showing no permeation. No data were available on the preferences and values of healthcare workers regarding the use of bleach/chlorine solutions for hand hygiene. However, input was gathered from GDG members, including professionals with field experience during the recent Ebola outbreak and those with extensive clinical experience from previous Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks. The second guidance document referenced was the 2016 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for Use in a Filovirus Disease Outbreak: Rapid Advice Guideline. This document was developed using the GRADE methodology and in consultation with a GDG. Several PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions were formulated, and rapid literature reviews were conducted, though no comparative studies were identified. Due to limited evidence on the effectiveness of different types of PPE, the GDG considered other information, including the values and preferences of healthcare workers regarding PPE. A WHO Collaborating Centre for Occupational Health conducted a literature review on healthcare workers' values and preferences for PPE but found limited information specific to Ebola disease contexts. The 2016 document targeted healthcare workers, such as doctors, nurses, and others providing clinical care or collecting samples from patients with suspected, probable, or confirmed filovirus infections. All recommendations from existing guidelines and interim guidance were reviewed, and a prioritization exercise was conducted with the GDG to identify which recommendations would be developed into new, formal recommendations or good practice statements, and which existing recommendations would be carried forward verbatim into the updated guideline. For recommendations carried forward verbatim, updated literature reviews were not conducted, as it was agreed during the guideline development process that new evidence was unlikely to emerge at this time. The focus was placed on higher-priority areas. Good practice statements were identified as foundational and reflected best practices in infection prevention and control (IPC). The GDG considered these statements essential for providing clarity and specificity to certain practices required to maintain safe patient care. These statements were reviewed and included in the document as good practice statements. During the development of PICO questions, five key background questions arose, and a rapid literature review was conducted to address them. While these background questions may not result in recommendations, they inform the GDG's decision-making process and have implications for implementation considerations. Examples of these questions include: What are the existing systems to classify the level of risk of exposure of healthcare workers to Ebola and Marburg viruses? What chlorine concentration and contact time are required to disinfect materials or surfaces contaminated with Ebola and Marburg viruses? What frequency of cleaning and disinfection is required for high-touch surfaces in facilities providing care to patients? A comprehensive search strategy was developed using combinations of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and text words for Ebola and Marburg viruses. Data sources included Medline, Embase, bioRxiv, medRxiv, Global Index Medicus, Epistemonikos, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data. Records from these sources were merged into a single database and screened using an automation tool (CAL® tool). Titles and abstracts were screened by a single reviewer after a calibration exercise, and full-text screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and evidence certainty rating using the GRADE approach were completed by a single reviewer with verification by an additional reviewer. The Knowledge Synthesis Team used study design-specific tools for risk-of-bias assessment. For randomized controlled trials, the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 Tool was used; for non-randomized studies, the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool was applied; and for observational comparative studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was employed. Results and evidence certainty were presented using GRADE Evidence Profiles and Summary of Findings tables. Due to a lack of data for pooling, a descriptive summary of patient characteristics, study characteristics, and risk-of-bias/methodological quality results was presented. Contextual data on cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, resource requirements, and feasibility were captured and summarized narratively. A review of the modes of transmission of Ebola and Marburg diseases was also requested. The Knowledge Synthesis Team conducted a rapid scoping review to address this question. Data sources included Medline, Embase, bioRxiv, medRxiv, Global Medicus Index, and Epistemonikos. The CAL® tool was used to identify potentially relevant systematic reviews and primary studies for screening. Full-text screening and data extraction were completed independently by a single reviewer with verification by an additional reviewer. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or arbitration by a third reviewer. As this review was scoping in nature, no quality assessments of included studies were performed, nor was the evidence for each outcome assessed for overall certainty. Data were charted against known modes of direct or indirect transmission and synthesized narratively by transmission modes (e.g., direct contact, indirect contact/fomite, droplet, sexual, vertical, airborne, and zoonotic). A mixed-methods study was conducted to assess the valuation of outcomes and contextual factors related to IPC measures for Ebola disease. This study included a quantitative online survey and in-depth qualitative interviews, guided by the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework. It aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of: 1. Valuation of outcomes relevant to IPC measures in the context of an Ebola outbreak. 2. Contextual factors related to decontamination and disinfection in managing Ebola patients. 3. Contextual factors related to PPE use in managing Ebola patients. Participants included key stakeholders, mainly from African countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea, with experience in Ebola management, as well as some participants from Europe. Stakeholders included decision-makers, WHO and UNICEF staff, representatives of NGOs, and healthcare workers with experience in Ebola disease management. Convenience sampling followed by snowball sampling was used to recruit participants. Members of the GDG and UN agencies were asked to share the invitation with their networks. Respondents to the online survey were also invited to participate in in-depth interviews. Ethics approval was obtained for the study.
